title: Spatial resolution and point spread function of high-resolution scanning SQUID microscopy probes
authors: Jan Ullmann, Katharina Kress, Timur Weber, Boris Gross, Daniel Jetter, Reinhold Kleiner, Martino Poggio, Dieter Koelle
abstract: Superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) show exceptional sensitivity to magnetic flux. In scanning SQUID microscopy (SSM), SQUID size and its distance to the sample are minimized in order to map weak magnetic fields with best possible spatial resolution. SQUID-on-lever (SOL) architectures have proven especially effective as SSM probes due to their small sensor size, robustness, and ease of integration with conventional atomic force microscopy hardware. In order to optimize magnetic microscopy carried out with SOL probes and to accurately reconstruct the magnetic fields that they measure, it is essential to know their point spread function (PSF). The size and shape of this PSF are determined by magnetic flux focusing effects, which depend on the characteristic length-scales of the superconductor and the sensor geometry. By simulating the coupling to sources of magnetic flux, this work provides a mathematical description of the SOL PSF, which contains a full description of the probe's magnetic sensitivity and spatial resolution. We then use measurements of a single magnetic skyrmion to measure the magnetic flux response of a real SOL. We demonstrate excellent agreement with flux responses that are obtained from simulations, thereby confirming the calculated PSF and spatial resolution.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive model to determine the Point Spread Function (PSF) of advanced Scanning SQUID Microscopy probes. By simulating magnetic flux coupling using superconducting circuit theory, the authors derive the PSF mathematically and validate it by comparing predictions against experimental measurements on magnetic skyrmions. This confirms the probe's intrinsic spatial resolution capabilities for nanoscale magnetic imaging.
main_problem: The primary goal is to accurately determine the Point Spread Function (PSF) of high-resolution Scanning SQUID Microscopy (SSM) probes for optimizing magnetic field mapping and image reconstruction.
main_result: The study provides a mathematical description of the SOL PSF, which was successfully validated by showing excellent agreement between simulated flux responses and measurements taken over a single magnetic skyrmion.
method: The research combines theoretical modeling using the Amperian-loop model (based on London theory) to simulate supercurrents and calculating the PSF via convolution/deconvolution techniques like the Landweber algorithm.
model_or_system: The physical system is a Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) patterned onto a lever tip (SOL architecture), used to map weak magnetic fields on samples like $	ext{Cu}_2	ext{OSeO}_3$. The analysis relies on calculating the coupling factor ($\phi_\mu$) from supercurrents.
key_observables: Point Spread Function (PSF), measured magnetic flux ($\Delta\Phi$), and spatial resolution quantified by FWHM.
important_parameters: SQUID size, sensor geometry, cantilever height ($h$), London penetration depth ($\lambda_L$).
main_assumptions: The Amperian-loop model is used for supercurrent simulation; the Landweber inversion process is sensitive to noise and missing low-frequency components.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics of the SOL probe, demonstrate PSF calculation from magnetic dipoles, and compare simulated vs. measured flux responses over skyrmions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need for PSF knowledge in SSM; it then details the simulation methods (Amperian-loop/Biot-Savart) to derive the mathematical PSF description; finally, it validates this model by comparing simulations against direct measurements on magnetic skyrmions.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the rigorous treatment of spatial resolution limits via deconvolution techniques and the comparison between simulation and experiment is highly relevant for any field requiring high-fidelity measurement reconstruction from localized probes.
